Bourgeois

boor-ZHWAH -- borrowed directly from French, describing a member of the middle class. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Bourgeois is of, relating to, or typical of the comfortable middle class; sometimes used to suggest excessive concern with material comfort and respectability.

Critics dismissed the sprawling suburban development as a symbol of bourgeois comfort and conformity.

Worked Example

A family carefully arranges matching furniture, a perfectly trimmed lawn, and a new car in the driveway, all chosen mainly to signal to the neighbors that they have arrived comfortably in the middle class.

That comfortable, status-conscious, middle-class conformity is exactly what bourgeois describes. Unlike 'aristocratic,' which implies inherited noble status, bourgeois describes an earned, middle-class respectability.

How Bourgeois Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

middle-class

middle-class: belonging to the social group between the working class and the upper class

conventional

conventional: following accepted social norms and standards

materialistic

materialistic: excessively focused on material possessions and wealth

Antonyms

proletarian

proletarian: relating to the working class

bohemian

bohemian: unconventional, especially in artistic or social habits

How Strong Is It? — middle-class → materialistic → bourgeois

middle-class vs. bourgeois

middle-class vs. bourgeois: Middle-class is a fairly neutral, descriptive term -- it simply names a social and economic group. Bourgeois can describe the same group, but often carries a slightly critical edge, suggesting excessive comfort or conformity.

materialistic vs. bourgeois

materialistic vs. bourgeois: Materialistic can feel more pointed than bourgeois: bourgeois broadly describes a middle-class way of life, while materialistic specifically criticizes an excessive focus on possessions and status.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -bourg-

root — -bourg-: town, fortified settlement (French (bourg), related to Old High German burg)

suffix — -eois

suffix — -eois: person of a place (French -ois) (French)

Put it together

Put it together: French bourg meant 'a town,' and -eois (the French ending -ois) marks a person who belongs to a place -- so a bourgeois was originally simply a town-dweller, neither peasant nor noble. Over time the word narrowed to the comfortable, property-owning middle class.

Use the root in a new word: borough
